utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before we have the opening statement, I'll ask the court deputy to give numbers to the documents that we mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Further to the oral decision by the Trial Chamber earlier today, D34 MFI will be Exhibit D34; D94 MFI will be Exhibit D94; D107 MFI will be Exhibit D107; D104 MFI will be Exhibit D104; D109 MFI will be Exhibit D109. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I also want to clarify the matter that was raised by the accused in relation to the time of his arrival and time of his departure and the fact that he has to wait for such a long time. It is essentially a matter for the Dutch government, but I quite understand the position of the accused and, indeed, of any human being who would find himself in a position where he has to sit and wait doing nothing for an hour and a half or two hours. The conduit between the Tribunal and the Dutch government in a matter such as this is the Registrar, and I will instruct the court deputy to bring this matter to his attention so that appropriate representations may be made to the Dutch government. Now, Mr. Tapuskovic, I understand that you will make an opening statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, about 20 days ago we had an opportunity to present some of our general views in respect of Rule 98 bis, and since I spoke about that at the time, I will not have to deal with that again now. I'm referring to what it was that I was saying then; namely, on the long-term campaign of shelling civilian sites and the civilian population of Sarajevo with a view to intimidating the population, killing it, wounding it, and committing inhumane acts against the civilian population. There is no reason for me to repeat any of what I said then. I believe that in my introductory remarks I would not have to give any particular assessments that rather belong to the final arguments in a case. I'm just supposed to indicate some of the elements that the Defence will deal with during its part of these proceedings. Again, I have to repeat that we were, indeed, in a delicate situation at the moment when we were deciding on the evidence we wish to call and today when we speak about all of that. Since we are still awaiting to see the fate of adjudicated facts. This has caused great difficulty for us, but I'm not going to dwell on that either. In a way, when I thought about my opening statement today, I really did bear that in mind, as well. During the Prosecution case, you heard a number of witnesses, I have to say that, and their statements primarily had to do with the experience of the victims. Of course, in such proceedings, that had to be dominant. What I can say is that none of these witnesses had seen soldiers in Sarajevo, none of them had observed weapons, none of these witnesses had observed any military activity from Sarajevo. According to what they said, this was a town of civilians that was exposed to horrid terror, where the only objective was killings, woundings, inhumane acts against civilians. I certainly understand all injured parties, so I'm not going to dwell on this any longer. Also, you heard a great many witnesses here who were policemen, who also know nothing about activity coming from town, who also did not see weapons, who also did not have occasion to note any serious activities coming from town. And, of course, at the end, one will have to assess what they had said, also in the context of what the Defence will have to say during its case. In their view, this was a civilian environment in which the police, like in any civilian environment, worked on crime investigations and they handled that the way they described it, with the difficulties involved due to the constant gun-fire that the town was exposed to. Of course, the Prosecution brought a number of witnesses here before you who were international observers from UNPROFOR and so on. When these witnesses testified, the Prosecution insisted only on the civilian dimension of the environment where all of this took place. I don't want to refer to all the witnesses called, but expert witness Donia said inter alia that indeed at that point in time, the town of Sarajevo was a civilian environment, and there's no need to repeat all of that now. However, at any rate, what dominants in the Prosecution's position is that this was a civilian setting inhabited by people who were exposed to the suffering referred to in the indictment. What the Defence will try to do is to bring in a number of people who were - and I'm not going to say on the other side of the front - but people who also lived in that town, also in the inner city that was a protected area for all, including those who lived in the inner city in certain areas that could not be separated that easily. These areas were also supposed to be treated as protected areas - that was the rule - and they experienced what they did, they will try to describe that here before you, and then you will be able to see all the facts, and you will be in a position to assess the responsibility of Dragomir Milosevic properly in this way. Of course, I'm not going to bring victims here because we are not in a position to do that. I am going to call here before you people who fought and who, throughout the war - and I have to look at the position of Dragomir Milosevic - who were in the area at the time. I cannot bring in policemen. I will perhaps call a single Defence witness who's a policeman who will be able to say to you that the same kind of investigations were conducted in other places within the inner city or on the other side of the front line, if I can put it that way, so that you know, at least up to a point, about what was going on on the other side as well. If I manage to, and I hope I will, I'm going to bring here before you a single witness who is a member of UNPROFOR, an international observer, who will be of assistance or should be of assistance in terms of clarifying one of the key incidents mentioned in the indictment. Let me now move on to this problem that particularly has to be accentuated. In the initial indictment, and not even in this amended indictment dated the 18th of December, 2006 - I'm trying to speak slowly because of the interpreters, because I did not provide any of this material to the interpreters in view of all the busy work we had. But nowhere in the indictment is there any reference to an armed conflict between the Sarajevo Romanija Corps and the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There is no mention of a clash between two armies in that area. It is true that my colleague Mr. Waespi -- well, sorry, it wasn't you, Mr. Waespi. You now have this difficult job ahead of you, but who actually said this -- the person who actually said this was Mr. Whiting. It was mentioned during the testimony of Mr. Donia, and he says the line of conflict was static, and the SRK held the line with a firm hand, although the army in Sarajevo had four times more soldiers than the SRK, they had 75.000 soldiers, and so on and so forth. At any rate, that is what was stated in Mr. Whiting's opening statement. However, I have to say, and I insist, that this was mentioned by way of an illustration, and that this fact remains that this armed conflict is not referred to at all in the indictment. Truth to tell, if you look at paragraph 26 of the indictment, it says: "At all material times relevant to this indictment, an armed conflict existed in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the territory of the former Yugoslavia." That was said at the very end of the indictment as a post scriptum, as if that had nothing to do whatsoever with Sarajevo itself. It was stated that that was a conflict that existed in Bosnia-Herzegovina in certain areas, or rather, that in the former Yugoslavia there was an armed conflict, but nowhere -- quite literally, nowhere in the entire indictment is there any mention of the armed conflict as a fact that did exist. And there is no mention in particular of the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as if it never existed. There is a single spot in the indictment, in paragraph 7, where it says that: "In Sarajevo hostilities broke out after Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised by the international community on the 7th of April, 1992." That is correct. But hostilities between who? Which two parties? It is never stated, and yet again they try to avoid stipulating that clearly, just as they did try to avoid mentioning the existence of an armed conflict. I understand that this may refer for April -- to April 1992 at the very outset, but during the material time when Mr. Milosevic was in command, what was in existence were both the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And to mention hostilities in such a way without going into detail and without mentioning facts that I hope will be proven through our case was responsible. I believe some of it was already corroborated by some of other witnesses during the Prosecution case. I believe the indictment cannot be viewed as such, unless it is corroborated by a decision from the Bench; only then can some importance be attached to the way it was phrased. In the same paragraph, it is also said that: "The city was subsequently subjected to blockade and relentless bombardment and sniper attacks. Bombardment and sniper attacks mainly came from positions in the hills around and overlooking Sarajevo, from which the attackers had a clear, detailed, and commanding view of the city and its civilian population." This is not the right moment to try and assess or guess who it was that was on the hills overlooking Sarajevo, who it was that took advantage of that geographical position during the material time. Because in the proceedings so far, we heard a lot about that. Therefore, I do not wish to state any position now. However, to state that a military crew was stationed for three and a half years up on a hill, whoever that hill belonged to, in order to have a commanding view of the civilian population, in my view - well, how should I put it? It is nonsense and I'm not afraid of using that word. To take up such position can only have a singular goal of obtaining a commanding view of enemy positions in a clash of two armies. It doesn't matter who occupied a particular hill because being positioned on a hill, having artillery there in order to target a civilian environment, well, that is beyond comprehension for any human. That is why at this moment I did not wish to comment on who it was on those hills. We will try to address that during our case within the authority that we have as Defence. To try and be direct, by our evidence, although we've heard some things during the Prosecution phase, we will try to show that throughout the material time, mentioned in the indictment against General Dragomir Milosevic, that there was a frontal as well as in-depth and in-width, an armed conflict with confrontation lines exceeding 200 kilometres where there was the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. These were the two armies present in the Sarajevo theatre as well as in the inner city, separated by Miljacka River. The separation line went through buildings, houses, front yards, literally. Along the entire front line, the two armies were very close to each other in their respective trenches. In such conditions in urban warfare, both warring parties inevitably had to sustain civilian casualties. Each of the parties were aware that any small-arms fire, any and every bullet or artillery projectile may cause death among civilians because these were settled areas. I wish to remind you of one sentence of one of the last witnesses we heard, the journalist, Martin Bell page 5253, lines 13 through to 21 of the transcript. He said: "I think that in one of my books I wrote down that there was no monopoly over human suffering, and this certainly pertained to the Serbs as well." This is what the witness stated. Defence --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was suffering of the civilian population within the area of responsibility of the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina due to the activities of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. That is what he said. We should also mention the 40.000 Serbs who remained in Sarajevo who did not flee because they were unable to leave with the 120.000 Serbs who had left Sarajevo initially. What we have today in Sarajevo is but 3 per cent of all the Serbs that lived there at the moment of the outbreak of hostilities, and this is a well-known fact. The civilian population within the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps suffered as well, due to the activities of the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Not only did they suffer and not only did they live in fear because of the combat activities, that was present on both sides, but also the Serb population suffered casualties. What Martin Bell said is a fact which needs to be weighed upon and taken into account when deliberating. This reciprocal suffering should be taken into account. This suffering being the consequence of an armed conflict between the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and the 1st of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and we will continuously point to that in our part of the proceedings. I want to make myself completely clear. The existence of such an armed conflict in which civilian casualties are unavoidable, of course that cannot be used as an excuse for targeting civilians directly, for sniping and shelling civilians exclusively. The same applies to any type of retaliation. It is completely out of the question. However, we need to take into account a representative sample of incidents in order to try and see whether that, indeed, happened the way it was described in the indictment. Unfortunately, as Defence counsel, I cannot offer evidence in that regard because we couldn't carry out our investigations in the city of Sarajevo itself. But based on the evidence we heard so far concerning many incidents, we may and can certainly provide our opinion in order to attach relevant importance to each and every piece of evidence. Another thing I wanted to mention is the following: In its indictment, the Prosecutor neglected the existence of an armed conflict and the inevitable fact of the loss of civilian life in such a conflict. It unilaterally ascribed all civilian casualties to only one side, describing as a campaign of intentional targeting of civilians, as if there was no armed conflict and as if it was an exclusively civilian area. What we could hear, for example, from the expert witness, Mrs. Tabeau, was that all victims in the heart of Sarajevo, even on the Serb side, she simply put together in a total number of victims. We have to keep pointing to the fact that there was an armed conflict in existence, and we will try to prove that the campaign, as discussed here, the armed campaign, was very much present on both sides, and especially during an important period of time, this being almost half of the time encompassed by the indictment against Dragomir Milosevic between May until end November, since that was the time of the offensive of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the NATO bombardment which ensued following an incident. We will put forth evidence, although we've heard some of that already, that that offensive did, in fact, exist and, by and in itself, it had to result in civilian casualties. Of course, I can only reiterate what I've already said, that no intentional targeting of civilians is permissible in trying to achieve one's military goals. And especially between May and November 1995, in my view, what one cannot distinguish between the campaign that existed and the one mentioned in the indictment as if there was no armed conflict and as if the SRK campaign went on by itself, as if there was nothing going on on the other side. All this made up for the entire context, describing the nature of the conflict at that moment. We will try to show that the fighting resumed after almost four months of truce, during which period there were certain minor incidents, irrespective of which side started them. And according to many witnesses and a lot of evidence, such a campaign on the BH side was well-prepared and long-lasting throughout the fall of 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Intentional targeting of civilians cannot be viewed isolated or separated from the rest of an armed conflict. If one wishes to prove something beyond reasonable doubt, one would need to show that, indeed, such targeting was intentional. However, although some examples were taken here as illustrations and portrayed as if the targeting was intentional, I am of the opinion that this was merely a consequence of a previous exchange of fire or in response of an intentional firing upon civilians on the part of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in order to achieve certain political or military goals, as Martin Bell put it before you, having said that no party had a monopoly over suffering. The same goes for any monopoly over truth concerning the events in that area, in that period. One needs to see things from one side and from the other side, especially in such areas where the warring parties were so close, like in the case of the Miljacka River. We heard witness Ghulam Mohatarem, and I wanted to point out his statement in particular at page 725 of the transcript, lines 12 to 25 and the first, second lines of page 726, I believe he was -- in answer to Mr. Waespi's question, I think he asked him whether the events when they took place were actually a stage that could have been viewed by the entire world - that was my interpretation - and that the world could learn the truth of those events the very same day. And when nothing was known about the casualties on the other side and, as Martin Bell said, he said that the television war was very present, that it was actually a televised war. It was a one-sided propaganda, stereotypes were being put into place, and it is difficult to deal with such circumstances even today, even as completely new arguments emerge. However, I'm convinced that this Chamber in this case, as in some other cases, will reach different conclusions after having heard evidence because such a monopoly over truth, as existed at the time, always resulted in a momentary judgement, which always, without exception, went against one of the parties. Such judgements were made on the very same day by the international public and the community by the most responsible political bodies of the UN and NATO, resulting in immediate action, be it sanctions or bombardments after each of such incidents that were learned of the very same day. This [indiscernible] to the events in Sarajevo. Let us just take three representative incidents described in the indictment and about which you are going to deliver your judgement. The terrible death of Nermin Divovic on the 11th of November, 1994, and the wounding of his mother, Dzenana Sokolovic with one single bullet, this is what the whole world learned about on the very day, and this truth still pertains and with this truth is -- the Prosecution case started. This was done by a terrible person, a criminal, from one location who managed to hit with a single bullet a mother and her child, wounding the mother and killing the child. There is another tragic incident which took place in Markale in which 40 people, according to the indictment, died, and another 80 were wounded. The judgement about this event was made on the very day, and the NATO started its humanitarian bombing, of course with aerial bombs, with blast effect, and depleted uranium, targeting civilian settlements as well. And we know that these aerial bombs, just like any other artillery weapon, cannot be very selective with engaging target. So the Defence is most definitely going to deal with these matters as well. And, finally, the event of the 28th of June, 1995, when an air-bomb hit the TV building in Sarajevo, killing one person and wounding a large number of people. As the Defence counsel of the accused Dragomir Milosevic, I believe that these incidents will show in a most convincing way why it is so important to examine the importance of each incident within the campaign through the prism of an armed conflict and the existence of a variety of interests and parties involved in the conflicts. I will talk about many other things when the time comes, but I would like to point out this issue because these were representative incidents chosen by the Prosecution, that the Prosecution used it as a basis to reach a conclusion which will just be extended from one case to another, by claiming that there was a campaign with a one single objective which was to kill, maltreat, and terrorise civilians, and there was suffering on both sides.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, the interpreter is asking you to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do that. A while ago I spoke about the witnesses that we need to call to appear before this Court for the Defence in order to establish certain facts, and they will be of assistance in that. You always have to establish beyond a reasonable doubt, and this is something that is most certainly the case. As far as I'm concerned, at the end of that horrible armed conflict, there was something that was relevant and important and it's something that His Honour Judge Robinson said himself, that even the First and Second World Wars bear certain relevance, but of course this cannot be of any significant relevance to this particular case. There are some influences of historical events and the fact that in 1991, 20 per cent of the population had survived the Second World War. But that cannot be a dominant fact when the time comes for the judgement. As Defence counsel and my colleague, we are working together on this, intend to bring here a historian, an expert witness, who I'm going to ask to -- just to describe to you the most important aspect and -- but this is not going to be of any significant influence on your judgement; nevertheless, I hope that this will be valued and evaluated in a proper way, at least when we are talking about geographical and demographical data. What the Defence intends to demonstrate in its case is that when speaking of the starting date of the period of responsibility of Dragomir Milosevic and his individual responsibility, which ended on the 25th of November, 1995, and began in August 1994, is something that can be of crucial importance and the key reason to establish his individual responsibility. My colleague put it in a conversation that we had: This should be a zero starting point that will lead to the determination beyond any reasonable doubt and under the given circumstances and within the time work to establish his criminal reliability. I'm not going to repeat the things I mentioned before, and I'm going to come back to them later. It is possible -- is it possible that in a criminal proceedings there can be an inherited culpability and guilt? This is not something that any criminal law recognises. Whatever it is, the only -- responsibility of a particular individual can be established, and only within the time-frame when something happened. This is the rule that is going to sustain as long as civilisation exists. Therefore, I have to point out only to the most significant aspects of the Defence case that pertain to these basic framework and circumstances prevailing in the time in question in addition to what I mentioned before. I'm not going to repeat anything about the campaign and what I said about the armed conflict, but I am going to talk about the period in which they have certain relevance and significance. Now, these specific circumstances are as follows, and I'm going to mention only the most important ones. Let me try to be concise and point out only those of utmost importance. When he assumed responsibility on the 10th of August, even before that - and that's an irrefutable fact - the Republika Srpska Republic of Srpska, somebody referred to it as the so-called Republika Srpska, which, in fact, was an area under the control of the people who had been living there ever since early ages when they came to this area. Sanctions were imposed by someone and this will have to be evaluated properly, and sanctions were imposed by the members of the same ethnic community and the international community as well. This caused a large number of problems relating to the supply of food, fuel, and everything else, but primarily relating to the things that were directly linked to this armed conflict, and by that I mean ammunition and weapons. A Serb Montenegrin aggressor was referred to at the beginning, but it is certain that according to the evidence called to date, on those delineation lines it is only people from that -- those areas that live there who stood on their own door-steps, in front of their own homes, guarding what they guarded as best they could. It was hard after such a long time for someone to think differently. Would a civilian in Sarajevo be a target. They have relatives there. So they -- their relatives were also victims. So under those circumstances, that's the way it was. However, we can say that there was this other very important new fact, and that is the Total Exclusion Zone, and it can certainly be stated that it was observed to the greatest possible degree, all the way up to May 1995, and it started in 1994. According to what witnesses said, international witnesses at that, all the way up to October this was observed and then there was some changes, there was some sporadic incidents, but at any rate this campaign -- sorry, not campaign but Total Exclusion Zone existed all this time. And what happened later on in May is a matter that will be discussed and that will to be proven here. And now whether that situation -- this was also infringed upon. Well, that is something we are going to deal with during the further proceedings and you're ultimately going to rule on that. In the view of the Defence, it is not disputable that from the moment when the accused, Dragomir Milosevic, took over his duty, this Muslim offensive started immediately after he assumed his duties in the summer of 1994, and this offensive in some form went on all the time. And then when there was a cease-fire -- and then when there was a cease-fire at the beginning of 1994, this cease-fire was used only to prepare a new offensive, and there was no question of continuing this cease-fire any longer. I'm not going to go into the political strategic reasons of any politician or any other person who was a decision-maker in this regard. I am talking about the people. I have to talk about soldiers as well, because they did not really meddle in politics or strategy and certainly not in history. Questions that were related to political matters, had there been reason on both sides, it is quite certain that this offensive would not have taken place at all, and there would have been many fewer casualties and victims, if any at all. However, a campaign, no way. That will be shown through the evidence that is to be called by the Defence and what happened during the war conflict of such intensity at that time, it will be for you to assess the significance of all of that. Then there is another matter, this domination over the hills that was referred to and that we will be dealing with. With the incessant use of the tunnel that existed at that time and through which soldiers went to their theatres of war, and there was a normal circulation of goods, people, food, everything else. After that, can one say that this was a milieu that could not meet its basic requirements because of activities launched from another side? It has already been proven that this tunnel was primarily used for military purposes and primarily to arm a particular environment that was supposed to be a demilitarised area at that period of time. And in terms of the Dragomir Milosevic indictment, it got even more equipment and became better equipped than the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps at the time Dragomir Milosevic was there. And they also had supremacy in terms of manpower and during the offensive it became even more dominant, perhaps the ratio became 1 to 5 or 6, rather than 1 to 3. We have already reached the stage that refers to the responsibility of the accused Dragomir Milosevic and the indictment against him. All of that will be shown through evidence, it led to a complete change of tactics of the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You heard about that here already, that the army was moving en masse outside the area of responsibility of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or rather, the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Within the inner city of Sarajevo, it was moving to other areas, and then there was activity down the entire front line, the front line being over 200 kilometres long. And I think that the witnesses we will be calling will testify about that, too. I just have to point out something that I've already said in a way; namely, that throughout this time that pertains to the period embodied in the Dragomir Milosevic indictment, there is absolute domination of the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the point of view of weapons and the quantity of ammunition used in combat operations, and we're going to prove that through documents of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which show how this was done and what the quantity of ammunition used was, especially in the time for which the accused, Dragomir Milosevic, was responsible. That means, and that is what I'm trying to say in this regard, is that only under such circumstances with the existence of an armed conflict and these circumstances that I've already described that prevailed at the time relevant to the indictment, can one refer to individual responsibility, individual criminal responsibility in keeping with the Statute of the International Criminal Tribunal. Another fact that is very important and that the Court has to deal with, and the Defence will focus on that in particular, is again related to Article 7 of the Statute, because on the basis of that article the responsibility of the accused is derived, that he planned the activities referred to in the indictment. In paragraph 19, this is particularly highlighted. I don't want to go back to that because it's hard for me to find the relevant passage. Because only when there is irrefutable evidence that such orders, such plans, existed, namely, to target civilians, terrorise them, torture them, and kill them, it is my understanding that that can only be established through the existence of written orders or irrefutable proof that somewhere such an order was issued verbally. In the Galic case - well, I'm not going to deal with that now, that should be dealt with at another point in time - what was taken as a point of departure was an interpretation of various conversations he had. And on that basis it was inferred that he directly issued such orders. I'm not going to analyse that now, but I believe that that cannot be just taken over, just like that. This need displayed by the Prosecutor to do that; namely, through agreed facts in the Galic case to get to these orders, these plans, in such a way, I think that that is basically untenable. In this case, you will not be able to establish through a single shred of evidence that there was such a direct order, that there was such a direct plan. You will not even be able to establish that he ever talked to anyone along those lines; namely, that it was necessary for such a plan to be carried through and implemented. If we look at any kind of inference process, I don't think it would be possible to simply take this over from another case, and I hope that this Trial Chamber is going to devote great attention to this if they look at that fact. As for the witnesses that will be called here before you, people that the accused saw every day and communicated with every day, they will be able to tell you about this, of course with the assistance of some of the documents that the Prosecution has. I think that one order that is referred to here and that was issued in the context of military activity after all, in anticipation -- well, the way it is, in anticipation of some attacks from the other side cannot be sufficient proof of such a crucial capital element indicating the existence of an order that would then pertain to Article 7 of the Statute of the Tribunal. Finally, I would just like to add a few more things. What was referred to several times here was whether the Defence insisted on certain matters that could pertain to the rule or principle of tu quoque. At one point in time, the Prosecution did not allow the Defence to deal with this at all. Of course, it never crossed the Defence's mind, because it would be pointless, to prove to you here what the number of killed soldiers was on the side of the Army of Republika Srpska. For us to bring you figures as in 2500 casualties, that would be pointless. However, witnesses will confirm that there was a great deal of loss of lives on the army -- on the side of the Army of Republika Srpska, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, that is. Or we're not going to bring you lists of civilians, but the witnesses are going to tell you about this. Just as people were killed in other areas, they were also killed in the areas where these people lived and where the soldiers of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps were. Least of all did we want to deal with the enormous number of Serbs who were killed, not by shells but who were the victims of the most serious crimes that were committed during this armed conflict. We are not going to prove that through our evidence, but if terror existed anywhere, it existed among the civilian population. Serbs, Croats, and Muslim civilians in Sarajevo were killed in this way, and the main fear was who would knock on your door tomorrow and who that would be and what would happen to you. We are not going to deal with that, but this fear that prevailed and the feelings of people who stood on their positions in front of their homes that they were defending could have been present as a particular element that could have motivated their perseverance in protecting themselves from such a thing. I did not oppose the Prosecutor when he admitted a large number of exhibits. I would just like to refer to one, P484, by way of an example. It has to do with information about the prevalence of crime in the zone of responsibility of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps where it says in a large number of these documents pertaining to individual months, and this is June 1995: "International law of war in terms of this type of crime in this relevant period, not a single criminal report was filed in this respect." Well, of course, it could not have been filed because in the zone of responsibility of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, there were no killings, there was no torture, there was no abuse of prisoners. Whenever people were taken prisoner, they were exchanged, either for other prisoners or for dead Serbs; that will be proven through our evidence. And no one was ever exposed to what the Serbs in Sarajevo were exposed to. From that point of view, that is what is stated in these documents. Another question that you will have to give serious thought to is whether in such a situation, especially during the course of this conflict between May and November 1995, could have dealt with investigations or was in a position to deal with the investigation of cases when shells were fired in such an armed conflict, and such shells could cause death and did cause death. Was that ever possible in any war when even physically one could not go to the other side? That will be for you to assess. But I indicated this dimension pertaining to that; namely, that in the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, there were no crimes like those that were committed against the Serbs in Sarajevo. That is one of the elements that is very important for the behaviour of the people who were members of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. And in my view, that cannot be tu quoque. Had there been such crimes, then tu quoque would be the case. Another thing that I believe is going to be important during the Defence case and something that was perhaps shown until now as well, is whether people who comprised the Army of Republika Srpska could decide just like that to target civilian areas of the city of Sarajevo, knowing that they had relatives, brothers, uncles, friends, the closest of friends living there. Is there any logic there, unless it was done when it simply had to be done? I repeat that any crime that was committed in terms of targeting civilians directly has to be punished; however, one has to make a distinction between such things. And let me finish, please. I don't know to what extent in this way we will manage to show during our defence case, some things have already been demonstrated even until now, this is what the conflict looked like. I'm going to finish by saying the following: I have here a document signed by Rasim Delic. I didn't want to refer to other documents, although I did have them. I hope that Rasim Delic will appear here before this Tribunal. In this document, it says -- and this is a document dated the 11th of July, 1995, the document is 3542, DD00 from our 65 ter list, that is. Can you see it? I would just like to read out the most important part of it: "In view of the fact that we have entered the fourth year of our war against the Serb Montenegrin aggressor and that there are well-known forms of combat activity, frontal, combined, and partisan warfare are not always useful, and our activities to date show that partisan type of combat actions within the same we use very little, although the deployment of our forces, particularly characteristics of the terrain enable that, and for the purpose of intensifying the partisan form of combat activities, active activities, and particularly combat action diversions, I hereby do order. "Up to the 15th of July, 1995, and in the basic zone of responsibility carry out all preparations for execution of diversion actions at the level of divisions." And then paragraph 4, and let me end by reading that out: "These tasks to be realised as frequently as possible and as deeply as possible to PZT and create with the enemy as great an insecurity as possible. Actions to be taken according to the system: Destroy and come back." If I have such an order in writing, then one should take into account, at least a bit, what I said, that such orders have to exist. And why is it indispensable to prove that there is an armed conflict? This is best shown by what we see here now. I wish to end on that note and to thank you for your attention, thank you for the time you've accorded me and these problems that we will be dealing with during our Defence case, so that you can make a valid decision at the end beyond a reasonable doubt. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll hear the first witness. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we go for a break now? First of all, we weren't able to show the layout of the courtroom to the witness, and I can regroup during the break and launch my examination more efficiently. The witness arrived quite late, and we couldn't have used the previous break for preparing him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll take the break now, 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And you may begin, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, can you tell me your first and last name, please.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Stevan Veljovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You know that I appear on behalf of General Dragomir Milosevic. I believe you are familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We met and discussed various matters on several occasions, particularly in such moments when we were still discussing your possible testimony; that is, whether you will appear before this Tribunal or not?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In order to move as expeditiously as possible through the examination-in-chief, I would kindly ask you to speak slowly and to wait for my question before beginning your answer since it is the only way to make good use of our time. Did you understand me?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It is best for you to look at the screen in front of you. When the cursor stops, that means that I have concluded my question or that you have concluded your answer. Did you understand that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber the year of your birth?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 29th of November, 1956.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us where?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: I was born in the village of Mislav at the tripartite border of the municipalities of Han Pijesak, Sokolac, and Rogatica, although we are in the Rogatica municipality. It was in the former Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about your education?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: By vocation, I am a wood-cutter and I process wood as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When did you complete your education?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us slow down a bit. Besides the education you mentioned, have you completed any other schools?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: As concerns my civilian life, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you that because it is of some importance for you to tell the Chamber whether you acquired some military knowledge as well.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: I completed the infantry school for reserve officers in Bileca in 1976 -- it was, rather, between 1976 and May 1977. The course lasted 15 months.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were you assigned a rank with the military?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Upon completion of that reserve officer's school, I became a reserve lieutenant second class.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At the time you were assigned that rank back in 1978, what did that mean -- excuse me, just wait until I have finished with the question and then start answering. Mr. Veljovic, I asked you what it meant at the time when you completed the reserve officer's school in 1978?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: It meant that I was to remain with the reserve forces as an officer, and I was supposed to be at the disposal of the then-Yugoslav National Army or the Territorial Defence. I occasionally received calls for exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please expand on that? Once you completed the school, what was your occupation? How did you make your living?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: I worked on my civilian job.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Veljovic, please bear in mind the cursor on the screen and do not begin your answer before it has stopped. As of 1978, did you earn your living working in the civilian sector?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As for your duties of a reserve officer, what did that comprise between 1978 and the moment of the outbreak of hostilities in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: According to the law that was in place, it was my duty that every four years I attend military exercises and to undergo additional training if summoned by the competent body.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What sort of a duty was it, a military one? I don't want to lead you in any way.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: In our country, there was a duty on the part of each and every able-bodied officer and soldier to serve in the reserve.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If you were, indeed, drafted every four years, how much time would you spend with the JNA on each occasion during those 12 or 13 years?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: We would remain there between seven and 30 days at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I will go back to that topic later on, but for the time being can you tell the Chamber what happened once the conflict broke out in 1992 as regards your duties; that is, your duties of a citizen?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Before the conflict, in February we were called by the competent ministries and bodies - and when I say "we," I mean the reserve officers and soldiers of Serbian ethnicity as well as Muslims and Croats - to report to our respective wartime assignment units.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In those units and in the areas where you went to attend exercises, who were the people who were called to assemble there?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: All able-bodied men, irrespective of nationality or ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Chamber what it looked like in practice, in real life?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Within the unit that I was assigned to, most members were Muslims and Serbs. There was a number of Croats. As for the officer cadre, we had other nationalities as well, including Slovenians and Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What period is it exactly?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: January, February, and March of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know of what was happening in some other parts of the former Yugoslavia at the time?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What was happening?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: There was a conflict between the Yugoslav People's Army and the Slovenian Territorial Defence. I also knew that there was a war in Croatia in 1991 waged between the Serbian and the Croatian people, as well as the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When you were mobilised in 1992, what were your hopes, expectations, as a reserve officer? What were the hopes you had vis-a-vis the army that was still in existence at the time?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Myself, as well as other reserve officers of other ethnicities, were of the opinion that there was -- there wasn't going to be a conflict between the citizens of Serbian, Croatian, and Muslim ethnicity in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How did you view your duty?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: With patriotism, since the state of Yugoslavia was still in existence, including all the republics. It was a state recognised by the UN and it was a member of the non-aligned movement, actually one of its founders.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us in brief what happened at a certain point in time? I don't want to lead you in any way. What happened within that organisation that used to be multi-ethnic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Up until May, most officers and soldiers of other ethnicities were still with their respective wartime units. On the 3rd of May, when the army command was pulling out of the city, it was attacked by some illegal armed formations called the Green Berets and the Patriotic League. What happened then was that many soldiers were killed, and then the soldiers and officers of other ethnicities began leaving their units for some other units of their own that I had no knowledge of.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber who were members of the Yugoslav Army up until that moment? I'm referring now to the people you knew personally and I am particularly now referring to the commanding officers.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: The deputy commander of my brigade was at the time Lieutenant-Colonel and currently Brigadier in the BH army, Asim Dzambasovic. In the operations and training organ, there was Major Nehru Ganic, currently a general in the BH Army. In the corps that we as a brigade were part of, the chief of the operations section was Rasim Delic; there was also Sefer Halilovic, Hadzihasanovic, and many others.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened with regular soldiers after the time that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Ordinary soldiers of other ethnicities put down their weapons and went home.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: I remained with my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What time specifically are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about April and May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was that still the regular army?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the Yugoslav People's Army until the 19th of May; after that date, the JNA had been ordered to withdraw to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: While the army -- the army command was pulling out from the Bistrik sector in Sarajevo on the 3rd of May, our task was to help members of the JNA to evacuate by providing them with vehicles, fuel, and other assets necessary for the pull-out and departure towards Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened with the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: The command of the Yugoslav People's Army was attacked by paramilitary units and did not manage, with the exception of a small number of members, to evacuate from Sarajevo. They were killed while they were in column, including soldiers and officers, and most of them were taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened after they had pulled out, the JNA?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: All the units that were not surrounded withdrew on the 19th of December towards the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; however, the units from Sarajevo failed to pull out of the Marsal Tito barracks. Those were cadets, and among them were other ethnicities, not only Serbs. They did not pull-out of the Viktor Bubanj barracks, too, as well as from the use of Djonlic barracks at Ali Pasin Most. They managed to get out only on the 5th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What was the position and the situation of the soldiers and barracks before June 1992?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: They were completely surrounded. They were being attacked, and concurrently there were negotiations about their departure from the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So once they managed to leave Sarajevo, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: They were sent in columns to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to continue their training, the rest -- except for the soldiers and officers who were originally for -- from Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any officers who were born in Serbia, but who nevertheless decided to remain in that area?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were, but very few of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Those who stayed behind, why did they decide to remain?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that the reason was that they spent their entire working life in Bosnia-Herzegovina, they were married to women from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they also had certain property, houses, land, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Chamber what was the status of the accused, General Dragomir Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: General Dragomir Milosevic was at the time a colonel. He had a flat in Sarajevo. He was married to a woman in Sarajevo from the Vogosca municipality. He had a weekend cottage in the general area of Mokro village in Pale municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And where was his flat?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: His flat was in the city of Sarajevo. As far as I can remember, the name of the neighbourhood was Socijalno. It was not very far from the Marsal Tito barracks, about 300 metres from the main street of the Sarajevo, between Cengic Vila and Marin Dvor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And do you know what happened with this flat?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly where it is, and I don't know what happened with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And where was his family at the time?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: In their weekend cottage in the village of Mokro in Pale municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened with the property of other JNA officers who for that time had been living in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, after they left their flats were occupied and they never managed to be granted restitution rights, although most of them had bought these flats according to the law and these flats were actually private property.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from the officers, what happened with the residents of Sarajevo who up until that time had been living in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Many citizens of the Serbian ethnicity left the town even before the war broke out. After the war broke out, those who did not leave and went to the Serbian-held territories were arrested, maltreated, and some of them were liquidated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did some people manage to get out of the city?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In what way?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: There were commissions set up at the level of Republika Srpska and at the level of the then-Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was also possible to leave the town with the assistance of UN forces, and there were other ways to leave the town since there were people who were well-connected and probably with some kind of remuneration they managed to be sent towards the Serb-held territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything at all about the existence of paramilitary formations in 1991?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: We knew about that. Particularly we, reserve and active-duty officers, were informed that the SDA party had begun organising paramilitary units under the name of the Patriotic League and the Green Berets, that they were arming themselves, that they were undergoing training, and that they were making preparations for armed attacks on Serbian villages, neighbourhoods, and the Yugoslav People's Army, and its depots filled with combat equipment and quarter-master equipment and assets.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What happened with these JNA depots?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: The depots that were being secured by the Yugoslav People's Army in April 1992 came under attack, specifically I mean the Faletici depot in the eastern part of Sarajevo, north-eastern part of Sarajevo, where equipment was stored belonging to the staff of the Territorial Defence of the city of Sarajevo. According to the information that we had, there were around 45.000 pieces of weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So what happened?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: When they entered the warehouses, and I mean the Patriotic League and the Green Berets, they started driving the weapons away and a conflict broke out between the local residents of Faletici, which included the villages Mrkovici, Bijoska [phoen], and Hresa, and the Muslim paramilitary forces; i.e., the Patriotic League and the Green Berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What was the conflict about?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: The dispute about who was going to take the weapons because members of the Patriotic League and the Green Berets started taking the weapons in large quantities, and that is when the Serbs started to take weapons themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, in order for us to be able to continue this examination-in-chief, can you turn towards the map behind you and do your best that while you are explaining the map to speak in the microphone, otherwise this exercise would be futile.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If possible, can the camera turn towards the map, so that we can see it on the screen and so that I can pose questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Veljovic, can you tell us, did you have anything to do with the making of this map?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about this a little bit later. In what way are you connected with the making of this map?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: I and a group of other officers worked on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In what capacity? Where were you at the time?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: At the time I was an operations officer in the staff of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what time-frame are we talking about and when did you assume that duty?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: I became an operations officer of the corps pursuant to an order issued on the 12th of December, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Who issued this order?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: It was issued by the corps commander, General Dragomir Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When did you assume your duty?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: I assumed my duties on the 19th of December, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you be more specific as to the time when this map was made, or at least give us an approximate date?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: This map was made in January 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Chamber all these inscriptions and writings that we can see on the map? What do they represent?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Each unit at a higher level must have its own documents. This also applied to the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Among those documents, one of the most important one was -- would be a military topographic map.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, I understand. But now can you explain at the time when you arrived at the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, you were given a task concerning this map. Can you explain in more detail?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Since in December 1994, a truce was signed between the Army of Republika Srpska and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina which lasted for four months, we in the staff started making and drafting all the necessary defence documents relating to our zone of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, I asked you a question and you gave me an answer, pursuant to whose order you did, who endorsed this, and what these signatures on the map mean, or rather, what the inscriptions in the map mean?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: This was approved by the commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, allowing the corps to make preparations for defence since there was intelligence indicating that a major offensive was about to take place by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina targeting the forces of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. I personally was tasked with, or rather, the whole staff, as a matter of fact, with preparing, drafting, the documents that would serve the purpose of defending our region, and part of this documentation is this topographic map. I personally received an order to this effect from the Chief of Staff, Colonel Cedomir Sladoje, and most probably he had been given an order, an oral order, by the commander, General Dragomir Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could we now try to explain to the Trial Chamber at this point in time at least the most basic things marked on this map. First of all, could you please explain what those two coloured lines denote?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: This is a military topographic map, 1:50.000 is the scale, which means that on this map 1 centimetre represents 500 metres in actual fact. This map shows the deployment of forces of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and it is marked in red. Also, there is the deployment of the forces of the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is depicted in blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If you look at these maps, they depict what you said but what else do these lines show as marked here?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: These lines show what the deployment forces looks like in the field in terms of artillery pieces and trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see - and I looked at this quite often - that line is interrupted. Can you explain that, what that means? Why is this line interrupted? Why is it not a whole line?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Such interrupted lines show that in this entire area, there were no dug-outs or trenches. It means that they had a dispersed deployment since neither the Sarajevo Corps or the corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina could not cover the line in terms of having one soldier next to another one in view of the size of the front line, especially the units of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. In terms of manpower, they had four times less than the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the 1st Corps had. The 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had, in terms of manpower, personnel, about 78.000 troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, you said the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, the corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, whereas the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was four times weaker in terms of human potential; it had 18.000 soldiers and officers, which shows that the ratio of balance of forces was 1 to 4 working in the favour of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How long was this line that is marked here in two colours; one colour on one side, the other colour on the other side?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: If we look at this from a professional point of view, a topographic map starts from 0. That means that everything is flat. Since Bosnia-Herzegovina is a very hilly terrain, this front, both sides was 245 to 250 kilometres long.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What can that mean then in view of the number that you mentioned a few minutes ago, the number of soldiers that the two respective sides had? What was the situation like at the separation lines on the basis of your knowledge and on the basis of what you've stated so far?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: In order to cover the entire front line, from a military point of view about 100.000 soldiers were needed in order to have a regular deployment in terms of combat disposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And how many persons were there?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: 18.000 soldiers of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps were there and on the Muslim front of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the 1st Corps, that is, there were 78.000 soldiers meeting all the requirements of that terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What else does this map depict when we look at the separation line in view of these topographic characteristics?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: What is very characteristic is something that I shall put to you now. The city of Sarajevo is surrounded by many mountains, some of them of Olympic calibre, and parts of the town of Sarajevo are on the slopes of these mountains; namely, Trebevic, Jahorina, Igman, and Ozren, as well as Romanija. If we look at the separation line here in the area of Igman, we see that the Muslim forces are predominant, that they are at an altitude higher than that where the forces of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps were deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: If we move towards the urban area, in the region of Hrasnica that was under Muslim control and in the area of the village of Vojkovici, which was part of Vukovica, they were at the same altitude. It's only 1 or 2 metres as these rivers flow into the Bosna River. If we move here towards the urban settlement that is called Dobrinja and above Dobrinja and all the way up to Lukavica and Vraca is the feature Mojmilo, where the forces of the corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were dominant. They were dominant at an altitude of above 150 metres in respect of the forces at Lukavica and the forces in the urban areas where the Serbs were; that is, Grbavica. If we go into the urban area, we see that our position is more or less the same in terms of altitude since we're close to the Miljacka river, both sides close to the Miljacka but not on it, then there is the hill of Debelo Brdo, an imposing feature held by the Muslim forces. There was cross-fire there, and they were firing all the entrances into Grbavica and Vrace, both from the area of Mojmilo and the area of Debelo Brdo. Further on, the line continues over Mountain Trebevic. This is a forested mountain. So the forces of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps are dominant; however, the evergreen trees there were between 10 and 20 metres high, so from Trebevic you cannot see the urban area, only one part where the funicular is and that area is 70 metres wide. It is from there that one can see this part of town. As for this part of Trebevic, the one covered in forest, that is where we were of a higher altitude; however, we could not see anything, we were in the forest together with the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In this area, the road leading to Pale, the Muslim forces were dominant, from the area of Colina Kapa, Zastavnik and Popovac. We are at a lower altitude. If we go further on towards Hresa and --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, please, Mr. Veljovic, could you take a look at a document pertaining to these matters precisely, D110 is the document. It was tendered by the Defence a long time ago. So could you have a look at that now, and could you link it up to what you've been telling us until now, D110? It will appear on the screen. Then, before you continue explaining this, could you have a look at the document and tell us whether what you've been saying corresponds to this document?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Could it please be enlarged a bit? Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The document that is on our screen is the court schedule, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: For us, we haven't received it yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He has the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it just be enlarged a bit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, may I ask the Prosecutor, do you have the document in front of you -- no, I mean on your screen? No. It's there now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, here it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it please be enlarged a bit? A bit more, please. Very well. Could you please lower it a bit? Yes. I cannot see the whole page.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could we please see both versions? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can read it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't have the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was there a few moments ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Veljovic, please have a look at the document and could you analyse it? Could you please give your comments to the Trial Chamber in relation to everything you've said so far before we continue with the questions?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I prefer if you put specific questions to the witness, rather than to invite him to comment generally, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you've just started explaining these topographic elements. What you've said so far and what is in this document, does it correspond to what you've been saying so far? I'm asking you this before you continue explaining the map further.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see now what all of this is, and can you explain what this is all about?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: This is what this document is about. All vital features, Grdonj, Borija, Colina Kapa, Debelo Brdo, Mojmilo, Azici, Stupsko Brdo, Vis, Zuc, the faculty of traffic and transport engineering must have wire communications from two sides. "Wire lines must be dug into the ground or extended along connecting trenches (depending on the cable and terrain, digging into connecting trenches is allowed). To implement paragraphs 1 and 2, chiefs of communications shall send an itemised list of equipment needed to the division," et cetera. "Chief of Staff Colonel Rizvo Pleh," and in the letterhead it says the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the 12th Army Division Command. So this confirms that they hold all vital features.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: The army, the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is what this document shows.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, can you continue from where you broke off?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I explained this. Grdonj, Borija, Colina Kapa, Debelo Brdo. Now, there's Hum, Zuc. This is a big feature, Zuc, from which there is a good view, that is the feature of Zuc; that is to say, facing Rajlovac and Vogosca, and from Hun towards Polje. So this is a very strong feature which controls the entire area here of the south-western front, right over here on this urban area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: These hills on the northern side in particular, on this northern side, is there a single position where the Army of Republika Srpska was and that you know of?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Not a single dominant feature on the north or the north-western part was under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska, or rather, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Court the position of the so-called Spicasta Stijena?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is where Spicasta Stijena is. It is above the settlements of Breka and Sedrenik and towards the village of Mrkovici. This part here from Spicasta Stijena down to Borija is a wooded area. There are small pine trees there, whereas the elevations such as Grdonj, Pasino Brdo were under the control of the 1st Corps. From the forested area and from that elevation, the forces of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps had no view of the settlements and the city, apart from one part here close to Spicasta Stijena they could see Kosovo and Polje, whereas in this part, they had no view whatsoever. That was the only direction they had any view of.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that. In addition to the northern side and the elevations you've indicated, can you show us the features important for the western side?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Going to the west, towards the west, there is the feature of Zuc, Hum and Zuc, two features. At those elevations there were units of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, of its 1st Corps, that is. They controlled and they were dominant because we were some 150 or 200 metres below. From this part we couldn't see Sarajevo at all because of the Zuc feature.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Continue?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Now we move on to Rajlovac and Ilidza. This is the railroad where more or less there was a balance because one has a view of both sides on both sides of the confrontation line. This entire part here up to Nedzarici and Kasindolska Street at the airport, there was a balance of forces, so to say, apart from a part of Nedzarici because at Mojmilo the altitude is greater and there were activities from this feature towards Lukavica and Dobrinja as well, that was the dominating feature.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, if I may. After all this explanation, for which locations can we say that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps had dominance over?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: The units of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps dominated in the area of Trebevic, in this part here, but this is all forests. We had no view of the city. The units of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, of its 1st Corps, were also in the forest; however, we were perhaps at a somewhat greater altitude of 20 to 50 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What was the distance between positions if we take a look at the red and the blue line? What was the actual distance between your position at Trebevic, at its highest point, and Colina Kapa only the other hand, for example?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: This is Colina Kapa. This is about 1500 metres. I would say between 800 and 1200 metres, I cannot be precise. I would have to have something to measure it with, and I was talking about Colina Kapa. There was no range for any pieces and they had no view of anything; therefore, they couldn't use them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What is an approximate distance between Colina Kapa and, for example, Marin Dvor?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Between Colina Kapa and Marin Dvor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please wait until I finish my question before you start answering. You can continue?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Colina Kapa to Marin Dvor. As the crow flies, it is about 4 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What is the distance between Zlatiste and Debelo Brdo?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: This is Debelo Brdo, this is Zlatiste.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If I may, according to the map who had Debelo Brdo under its control?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: According to the map and according to the documents signed by the commander of the 12th Division, units of the 12th Division were there and they were part of the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as stated in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Compared to Debelo Brdo, where is Zlatiste?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Zlatiste is around 3 or 400 metres away from Debelo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What is the difference in altitude between the two features?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: This feature of Debelo Brdo is shaped in such a way that from Zlatiste you cannot see much of this part of the city; however, you can see the other part of the city which is on the other side of the Miljacka River. The distance is around 1500 metres as the crow flies or maybe 2.000 metres, depending on the layout of terrain. The map is flat. The topographic reference point is 0, but if we take into account the actual fact, the layout of the terrain, the distance is much greater.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When we look at the entire line you were mentioning, along that line what is the only place where we could say that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps units dominated at?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Only in the area of Trebevic, which is forested; and as such, one cannot open fire precisely at the positions of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or could they also open effective fire since they were also in the forested area?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Explain, please.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is difficult to fight in the woods. One cannot aim precisely and one cannot target personnel or embankments, since the trees prevent you from doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In the relevant period --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: There were no changes in terms of positions from 1992 until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will cut my examination short tomorrow. I would just kindly ask you if we could break now since I am exhausted, and I will make up for the time lost tomorrow -- or on Monday, I guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So we are not resuming tomorrow, we will resume on Tuesday, the 29th. Monday's a holiday. But we can break now. We'll break now and we'll resume on --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll resume at 9.00 a.m. on Tuesday, the 29th, in Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 29th day of May, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.54 p.m.,
